coupon year 2          3.56
coupon year 3          3.36
coupon year 4          3.17
coupon year 5          2.99
face value, year 5    74.73
The price is the sum of these 6 present values.


D1 (b). Compute the price.
\[P = 4 \times \frac{1-(1.06)^{-5}}{0.06} + \frac{100}{(1.06)^5}\]

coupon, face, y, years = 0.04, 100, 0.06, 5
annuity_factor = (1 - (1 + y) ** -years) / y        # 4.212364
coupons_pv = coupon * face * annuity_factor         # 16.85
face_pv = face / (1 + y) ** years                   # 74.73
P_d1 = coupons_pv + face_pv
print(f"annuity factor {annuity_factor:.6f}, coupons {coupons_pv:.2f}, face {face_pv:.2f}")
close(annuity_factor, 4.212364, 1e-6); close(coupons_pv, 16.85); close(face_pv, 74.73)
close(P_d1, 91.58)
print(f"The bond's price is €{P_d1:.2f}.")

annuity factor 4.212364, coupons 16.85, face 74.73
The bond's price is €91.58.


D1 (c). Is it at a premium or a discount, and why?

coupon, y = 0.04, 0.06
status = "premium" if coupon > y else ("par" if coupon == y else "discount")
assert status == "discount" and P_d1 < 100
print(f"A {status}: the bond pays {coupon:.0%} on its face while the market demands {y:.0%}, "
      f"so it must sell below €100 (here €{P_d1:.2f}) to make up the difference.")

A discount: the bond pays 4% on its face while the market demands 6%, so it must sell below €100 (here €91.58) to make up the difference.


D2 (a). The same bond (5 years, 4% coupon) at a yield of 4%, then at 2%. Both prices.

coupon, face, years = 0.04, 100, 5
for y, expected in [(0.04, 100.00), (0.02, 109.43)]:
    annuity_factor = (1 - (1 + y) ** -years) / y
    coupons_pv = coupon * face * annuity_factor
    face_pv = face / (1 + y) ** years
    P = coupons_pv + face_pv
    print(f"yield {y:.0%}: {coupon*face:.0f} × {annuity_factor:.6f} + {face_pv:.2f} = €{P:.2f}")
    close(P, expected)
print(f"At 4% the bond is at par (€100.00); at 2% it costs €{P:.2f}.")

yield 4%: 4 × 4.451822 + 82.19 = €100.00
yield 2%: 4 × 4.713460 + 90.57 = €109.43
At 4% the bond is at par (€100.00); at 2% it costs €109.43.


D2 (b). State the rule that connects coupon, yield and price.

coupon = 0.04
rows = []
for y in (0.02, 0.04, 0.06):
    P = price(coupon, 5, y)
    status = "premium" if P > 100 + 1e-9 else ("par" if abs(P - 100) < 1e-9 else "discount")
    rows.append({"coupon": coupon, "yield": y, "price": round(P, 2), "status": status})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
assert [r["status"] for r in rows] == ["premium", "par", "discount"]
print("Rule: coupon > yield → premium; coupon = yield → par; coupon < yield → discount. "
      "Price and yield always move in opposite directions.")

 coupon  yield  price   status
   0.04   0.02 109.43  premium
   0.04   0.04 100.00      par
   0.04   0.06  91.58 discount
Rule: coupon > yield → premium; coupon = yield → par; coupon < yield → discount. Price and yield always move in opposite directions.


D3 (resit form). A bond trades above par. Therefore: (i) its coupon is above its yield (ii) its yield is above its coupon (iii) it must be close to maturity.

# Check each alternative on a 4% coupon bond at a few yields and maturities
premium_cases = [(y, n) for y in (0.02, 0.04, 0.06) for n in (2, 10, 30)
                 if price(0.04, n, y) > 100 + 1e-9]
print("Above par only when (yield, years) =", premium_cases)
assert all(y < 0.04 for y, _ in premium_cases)          # (i) always holds
assert any(n == 30 for _, n in premium_cases)           # (iii) fails: 30 years out, still a premium
print("Answer (i): its coupon is above its yield — investors pay more than face "
      "only to obtain a coupon better than the going rate.")

Above par only when (yield, years) = [(0.02, 2), (0.02, 10), (0.02, 30)]
Answer (i): its coupon is above its yield — investors pay more than face only to obtain a coupon better than the going rate.


D4 (a). A zero-coupon bond pays €100 in 8 years. The yield is 5%. Its price today.
\[P = \frac{100}{(1.05)^8}\]

face, years, y = 100, 8, 0.05
growth = (1 + y) ** years             # 1.477455
P_zero_5 = face / growth
close(growth, 1.477455, 1e-6); close(P_zero_5, 67.68)
print(f"(1.05)^8 = {growth:.6f}, so the price is €{P_zero_5:.2f}.")

(1.05)^8 = 1.477455, so the price is €67.68.


D4 (b). If the yield rises to 6%, the new price and the percentage change.

face, years, y_new = 100, 8, 0.06
growth = (1 + y_new) ** years         # 1.593848
P_zero_6 = face / growth
pct_change = (round(P_zero_6, 2) - round(P_zero_5, 2)) / round(P_zero_5, 2)
close(growth, 1.593848, 1e-6); close(P_zero_6, 62.74); close(pct_change, -0.0730, 1e-4)
print(f"New price €{P_zero_6:.2f}; change ({P_zero_6:.2f} − {P_zero_5:.2f})/{P_zero_5:.2f} = {pct_change:.2%}.")

New price €62.74; change (62.74 − 67.68)/67.68 = -7.30%.


D5 (a). For the 5-year 4% bond priced at a 6% yield (D1): compute Macaulay duration, showing the weight of each cash flow.
\[D = \sum_t t \cdot w_t, \qquad w_t = \frac{PV_t}{P}\]

table = cash_flow_table(0.04, 5, 0.06)
P = table["PV"].sum()
table["weight"] = table["PV"] / P
table["t·w"] = table["t"] * table["weight"]
print(table.round(4).to_string(index=False))
print(f"sum of PV = {P:.2f}, sum of weights = {table['weight'].sum():.4f}")
D_mac = table["t·w"].sum()              # same as table["t·PV"].sum() / P
close(table["weight"].sum(), 1.0, 1e-9); close(D_mac, 4.611, 0.001)
print(f"Macaulay duration = {D_mac:.2f} years: the PV-weighted average time to being repaid, "
      "under five because the coupons come back earlier.")

D5 (b). Convert it to modified duration.
\[D_{mod} = \frac{D}{1+y}\]

y = 0.06
D_mod = D_mac / (1 + y)
close(D_mod, 4.350, 0.001)
print(f"Modified duration = {D_mac:.4f} / {1 + y} = {D_mod:.3f} (drills.md: 4.611/1.06 = 4.350).")

Modified duration = 4.6106 / 1.06 = 4.350 (drills.md: 4.611/1.06 = 4.350).


D5 (c). Estimate the price change if the yield rises by 50 basis points.
\[\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D_{mod}\,\Delta y\]

dy = 0.005                              # 50 basis points
pct = -D_mod * dy                       # −2.17%
dP = round(pct * P_d1, 2)               # rounded to the cent, as on paper: −1.99
P_new = round(P_d1, 2) + dP
close(pct, -0.02175, 1e-4); close(dP, -1.99); close(P_new, 89.59)
print(f"ΔP/P ≈ −{D_mod:.3f} × {dy} = {pct:.2%}, i.e. about −€{-dP:.2f}, "
      f"giving roughly €{P_new:.2f}.")

ΔP/P ≈ −4.350 × 0.005 = -2.17%, i.e. about −€1.99, giving roughly €89.59.


D6 (a). A 10-year bond with a 5% coupon trades at par (yield 5%). Its modified duration is 7.72. Estimate the new price if the yield rises to 6%.

P0, D_mod_10, dy = 100, 7.72, 0.01
# Check the given 7.72 from the cash flows (Macaulay / (1 + y))
table = cash_flow_table(0.05, 10, 0.05)
print(table.round(4).to_string(index=False))
close(table["t·PV"].sum() / table["PV"].sum() / 1.05, 7.72, 0.005)
P_dur_only = P0 * (1 - D_mod_10 * dy)
close(P_dur_only, 92.28)

D6 (b). The actual price at 6% is €92.64. Compare, and say which way the estimate errs.

P_actual = price(0.05, 10, 0.06)        # recompute the "actual" price ourselves
close(P_actual, 92.64)
gap = P_actual - P_dur_only
close(gap, 0.36)

      "Duration alone overstates the loss (and understates the gain when yields fall).")

D7 (stretch). Order by duration, longest first: (i) a 10-year zero-coupon bond (ii) a 10-year 8% coupon bond (iii) a 3-year 8% coupon bond.

# The drill gives no yield: any yield gives the same order; we try three.
bonds = {"(i) 10y zero": (0.0, 10), "(ii) 10y 8%": (0.08, 10), "(iii) 3y 8%": (0.08, 3)}
for y in (0.03, 0.05, 0.08):
    mac = {}
    for name, (c, n) in bonds.items():
        t = cash_flow_table(c, n, y)
        mac[name] = t["t·PV"].sum() / t["PV"].sum()
    print(f"y = {y:.0%}: " + ", ".join(f"{k} {v:.2f}" for k, v in mac.items()))
    assert mac["(i) 10y zero"] > mac["(ii) 10y 8%"] > mac["(iii) 3y 8%"]
print("Order (i) > (ii) > (iii): a zero's duration is its full maturity, coupons pull "
      "(ii)'s average forward, and (iii) returns the money in three years instead of ten.")

y = 5%: (i) 10y zero 10.00, (ii) 10y 8% 7.54, (iii) 3y 8% 2.79
y = 8%: (i) 10y zero 10.00, (ii) 10y 8% 7.25, (iii) 3y 8% 2.78
Order (i) > (ii) > (iii): a zero's duration is its full maturity, coupons pull (ii)'s average forward, and (iii) returns the money in three years instead of ten.


D8 (a). Using the D6 bond (\(P = 100\), \(D_{mod} = 7.72\), convexity \(C = 75.0\)), estimate the price at a yield of 6% using duration and convexity.
\[\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D_{mod}\,\Delta y + \tfrac{1}{2}\,C\,(\Delta y)^2\]

P0, D_mod_10, C, dy = 100, 7.72, 75.0, 0.01
duration_term = -D_mod_10 * dy          # −0.0772
convexity_term = 0.5 * C * dy ** 2      # +0.00375
pct = duration_term + convexity_term    # −0.07345
P_dur_conv = P0 * (1 + pct)
close(pct, -0.07345, 1e-9); close(P_dur_conv, 92.66)
print(f"ΔP/P ≈ {duration_term:.4f} + {convexity_term:.5f} = {pct:.5f}, so P ≈ €{P_dur_conv:.2f}.")

ΔP/P ≈ -0.0772 + 0.00375 = -0.07345, so P ≈ €92.66.


D8 (b). Compare with the actual €92.64 and with the duration-only estimate from D6.

err_dur = P_dur_only - P_actual         # about −0.36: below the truth
err_both = P_dur_conv - P_actual        # about +0.02: above the truth
close(err_dur, -0.36); close(err_both, 0.02)
print(pd.DataFrame({"estimate": ["duration only", "duration + convexity", "actual"],
                    "price €": [round(P_dur_only, 2), round(P_dur_conv, 2), round(P_actual, 2)]}
                   ).to_string(index=False))
print(f"Duration alone is €{abs(err_dur):.2f} below the truth; adding convexity leaves it only "
      f"€{err_both:.2f} above. The second term recovers almost all the curvature.")

            estimate  price €
       duration only    92.28
duration + convexity    92.66
              actual    92.64
Duration alone is €0.36 below the truth; adding convexity leaves it only €0.02 above. The second term recovers almost all the curvature.


D9 (the Board sentence). In two sentences, no formulas: what does convexity buy the holder of a bond, and why does a risk manager care about it?

# Show it on the D6 bond: yields up 1% and down 1%
for dy in (+0.01, -0.01):
    actual = price(0.05, 10, 0.05 + dy)
    straight_line = 100 * (1 - 7.72 * dy)
    print(f"yield {dy:+.0%}: actual €{actual:.2f}, duration line €{straight_line:.2f}, "
          f"holder better off by €{actual - straight_line:.2f}")
    assert actual > straight_line       # the curve beats the line on both sides
print("Convexity bends the price curve in the holder's favour: gains are bigger and losses "
      "smaller than duration predicts. A risk manager cares because a duration-only report "
      "overstates losses, and between equal durations the more convex bond is worth more.")

yield +1%: actual €92.64, duration line €92.28, holder better off by €0.36
yield -1%: actual €108.11, duration line €107.72, holder better off by €0.39
Convexity bends the price curve in the holder's favour: gains are bigger and losses smaller than duration predicts. A risk manager cares because a duration-only report overstates losses, and between equal durations the more convex bond is worth more.


D10 (stretch). Two bonds have the same duration; one has higher convexity. Rates move sharply, direction unknown. Which would you rather hold, and why?

D_mod, C_low, C_high = 7.72, 40.0, 75.0     # same duration, different convexity
for dy in (-0.02, +0.02):                   # a sharp move either way
    low = 100 * (1 - D_mod * dy + 0.5 * C_low * dy ** 2)
    high = 100 * (1 - D_mod * dy + 0.5 * C_high * dy ** 2)
    print(f"yield {dy:+.0%}: less convex €{low:.2f}, more convex €{high:.2f}")
    assert high > low                       # the convex bond wins in both directions
print("The more convex one: same behaviour for small moves, but for a large move either way "
      "it gains more and loses less. That asymmetry is worth paying for.")

yield -2%: less convex €116.24, more convex €116.94
yield +2%: less convex €85.36, more convex €86.06
The more convex one: same behaviour for small moves, but for a large move either way it gains more and loses less. That asymmetry is worth paying for.


D11 (a). Arno Bikes holds €400,000 of the D6 bond (at par) and €600,000 of a 2-year bond with modified duration 1.90. The portfolio’s modified duration, weighting by market value.

                         "market value €": [400_000, 600_000],
                         "modified duration": [7.72, 1.90]})
V = holdings["market value €"].sum()
holdings["weight"] = holdings["market value €"] / V
holdings["weight × D_mod"] = holdings["weight"] * holdings["modified duration"]

loss = -D_port * dy * V

share = -loss / V
ten_year_part = 0.4 * 7.72 * dy * V         # the part of the loss from the ten-year bond
print(f"Loss {share:.1%} of the reserve; €{ten_year_part:,.0f} of it comes from the ten-year holding.")

"A one-point rise in yields costs the reserve about €42,000, a little over 4% of it; about three quarters of the exposure sits in the ten-year holding, and shortening that would cut it roughly in half."


D12 (a). Arno Bikes must pay €500,000 in exactly 3 years; 1-year and 5-year zeros both yield 4%. How much must it set aside today?
\[PV = \frac{500{,}000}{(1.04)^3}\]

L12, y12, h12 = 500_000, 0.04, 3
growth = (1 + y12) ** h12                 # 1.124864
PV12 = L12 / growth
close(growth, 1.124864, 1e-6); close(PV12, 444_498.18)
print(f"(1.04)^3 = {growth:.6f}, so Arno Bikes sets aside €{PV12:,.2f} today.")

D12 (b). What share goes into each zero so that the portfolio’s duration is 3 years?
\[1\cdot w + 5\,(1-w) = 3\]

import sympy as sp
w = sp.symbols("w")
w12 = sp.solve(sp.Eq(1*w + 5*(1 - w), 3), w)[0]      # a zero's duration is its maturity
assert w12 == sp.Rational(1, 2)
print(f"w = {w12}: half in the 1-year zero, half in the 5-year zero (duration 1·½ + 5·½ = 3).")

w = 1/2: half in the 1-year zero, half in the 5-year zero (duration 1·½ + 5·½ = 3).


D12 (c). The euros in each, and the amount each zero pays at maturity.

each = round(PV12 / 2, 2)
face1 = round(each * (1 + y12), 2)        # paid in year 1
face5 = round(each * (1 + y12) ** 5, 2)   # paid in year 5
close(each, 222_249.09); close(face1, 231_139.05); close(face5, 270_400.00)
print(f"€{each:,.2f} in each; the 1-year zero pays €{face1:,.2f} in year 1, "
      f"the 5-year zero €{face5:,.2f} in year 5.")

D13 (a), (b), (c). Yields jump to 5% the day after the purchase. Value at year 3 of each zero, the total against €500,000; then the same with 3%.

rows = []
for y_new in (0.05, 0.03):
    reinvested = round(face1 * (1 + y_new) ** 2, 2)   # year-1 payment, reinvested for two years
    sold = round(face5 / (1 + y_new) ** 2, 2)         # 5-year zero with two years left to run
    total = reinvested + sold
    rows.append({"yield after": f"{y_new:.0%}", "1-year zero at year 3": reinvested,
                 "5-year zero at year 3": sold, "total": round(total, 2), "vs €500,000": round(total - L12, 2)})

close(rows[0]["1-year zero at year 3"], 254_830.80); close(rows[0]["5-year zero at year 3"], 245_260.77)
close(rows[0]["total"], 500_091.57); close(rows[1]["total"], 500_093.35)

      f"All in the 1-year zero, a fall to 3% would leave €{unmatched:,.2f} — €{L12 - unmatched:,.0f} short.")

D14 (b). The share in the 2-year zero that makes the portfolio’s duration 4 years, and the euros in each.
\[2w + 5.33\,(1-w) = 4\]

w14 = (D14 - 4) / (D14 - 2)

close(w14, 0.40, 0.005)

D14 (c). One year later, yields unchanged: by how much did each duration fall, and what must the treasurer do?

title: MBA03 · Week 7 — Three shapes, and how to decide with them
text:
European School of Economics · Mon 9 Nov 2026 · online · Tutor: Vincenzo Nardelli
Thursday gave each unknown number at Arno Bikes a mean and a spread. Today gives it a shape — and a shape is something you can read a probability off. Three shapes cover almost every number a firm does not know: a count out of \(n\) (binomial), a count at a rate (Poisson), a measurement (the normal). The founder’s four questions: how many of Saturday’s riders buy; what range to print on the box; which battery supplier to sign; how many of 250 orders will ship late.
This notebook is driven by the tutor. Every picture is followed by the same computation by hand on paper: formula, substitution, number, one sentence for the Board. The code is optional and not examined.
# Setup (Colab has plotly, numpy, pandas and scipy preinstalled; this is a no-op there)
import subprocess, sys
try:
    import plotly
except ImportError:
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", "plotly"])
import math
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
import plotly.graph_objects as go

RED, GOLD, GREY, INK = "#AF1F25", "#CDBA80", "#7a7f85", "#363636"
print("ready")

ready

title: MBA03 · Week 7 — Three shapes, and how to decide with them
section: A. How many of Saturday’s riders buy? — binomial, Poisson, one family
text:
A. How many of Saturday’s riders buy? — binomial, Poisson, one family
Saturday: 12 test rides. From the CRM, one rider in four buys (\(p = .25\)), and each decides alone. A fixed number of yes/no trials, the same \(p\) each time, independent: the binomial.
\[P(x) = \binom{n}{x}\, p^{x}\, (1-p)^{n-x} \qquad E(x) = np \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{np(1-p)}\]
Business reading: \(\binom{n}{x}\) counts the ways to pick which \(x\) of the \(n\) riders buy; \(p^{x}\) says those \(x\) all buy; \((1-p)^{n-x}\) says the others all do not. Four steps, every binomial question. “At least one” is always \(1 -\) “none”.
Below the four steps, two sliders, one at a time: the number of test rides \(n\) (with \(p = .25\)) and the share who buy \(p\) (with \(n = 12\)). Push \(n\) to 40 and watch the bars become a bell; drop \(p\) to .05 and see where the peak goes.

def binomial_steps(n, x, p):
    ways = math.comb(n, x); yes = p ** x; no = (1 - p) ** (n - x)
    print(f"1. the ways to pick which {x} of the {n} buy:   C({n},{x}) = {ways}")
    print(f"2. those {x} buy:                              {p}^{x} = {yes:.6f}")
    print(f"3. the other {n-x} do not:                      {1-p}^{n-x} = {no:.4f}")
    print(f"4. multiply:                                 {ways} × {yes:.6f} × {no:.4f} = {ways*yes*no:.3f}")
    return ways * yes * no

n, p = 12, .25
P3 = binomial_steps(n, 3, p)
print(f"\nscipy agrees: binom.pmf(3, 12, .25) = {stats.binom.pmf(3, n, p):.3f}")
print(f"\nmean          np = {n} × {p} = {n*p:g} buyers")
print(f"st. dev.  √np(1−p) = √({n} × {p} × {1-p}) = √{n*p*(1-p):g} = {math.sqrt(n*p*(1-p)):g}")
P0 = (1 - p) ** n
print(f"nobody buys   P(0) = C(12,0) × .25^0 × .75^12 = {1-p}^{n} = {P0:.3f}")
print(f"at least one  1 − P(0) = 1 − {P0:.3f} = {1 - P0:.3f}")
print("\nReading: one Saturday in four ends with exactly three buyers; nobody buying is a one-in-thirty Saturday.")

1. the ways to pick which 3 of the 12 buy:   C(12,3) = 220
2. those 3 buy:                              0.25^3 = 0.015625
3. the other 9 do not:                      0.75^9 = 0.0751
4. multiply:                                 220 × 0.015625 × 0.0751 = 0.258

scipy agrees: binom.pmf(3, 12, .25) = 0.258

mean          np = 12 × 0.25 = 3 buyers
st. dev.  √np(1−p) = √(12 × 0.25 × 0.75) = √2.25 = 1.5
nobody buys   P(0) = C(12,0) × .25^0 × .75^12 = 0.75^12 = 0.032
at least one  1 − P(0) = 1 − 0.032 = 0.968

Reading: one Saturday in four ends with exactly three buyers; nobody buying is a one-in-thirty Saturday.



ns = list(range(4, 41, 2)); ps = np.round(np.arange(0.05, 0.96, 0.05), 2)

def pmf_bars(n, p, visible):
    xs = np.arange(0, n + 1); ys = stats.binom.pmf(xs, n, p)
    return [go.Bar(x=xs, y=ys, marker_color=RED, visible=visible, name=f"n={n}, p={p}", showlegend=False),
            go.Scatter(x=[n * p, n * p], y=[0, ys.max() * 1.08], mode="lines", visible=visible, showlegend=False,
                       line=dict(color=GOLD, width=3, dash="dash"), name=f"mean {n*p:.1f}")]

fig = go.Figure()
for n_ in ns:
    fig.add_traces(pmf_bars(n_, .25, n_ == 12))
for p_ in ps:
    fig.add_traces(pmf_bars(12, p_, False))
T = 2 * (len(ns) + len(ps))
def vis(idx):                       # show the pair of traces number idx, hide all others
    v = [False] * T; v[2*idx] = v[2*idx + 1] = True; return v
steps_n = [dict(method="update", label=str(n_), args=[{"visible": vis(i)},
           {"title": f"n = {n_} test rides, p = .25 → mean np = {n_*.25:.1f}, σ = {math.sqrt(n_*.25*.75):.2f}"}]) for i, n_ in enumerate(ns)]
steps_p = [dict(method="update", label=f"{p_:.2f}", args=[{"visible": vis(len(ns) + i)},
           {"title": f"n = 12 test rides, p = {p_:.2f} → mean np = {12*p_:.1f}, σ = {math.sqrt(12*p_*(1-p_)):.2f}"}]) for i, p_ in enumerate(ps)]

                  xaxis_title="number of buyers", yaxis_title="probability", xaxis_range=[-0.5, 40.5],
                  sliders=[dict(active=ns.index(12), steps=steps_n, currentvalue=dict(prefix="n (p = .25): "), y=-0.05),
                           dict(active=int(np.argmin(abs(ps - .25))), steps=steps_p, currentvalue=dict(prefix="p (n = 12): "), y=-0.35)],
                  margin=dict(b=200))
fig.show()

Small n: count the ways. Large n: the bars smooth into a bell — block D uses that. Tiny p with many trials: a Poisson.



Poisson: the helpline, three calls an hour
Calls arrive at random, 3 an hour. The one person answering steps out for half an hour. A count in an interval, constant rate, no ceiling: the Poisson. Write \(\mu\) = rate × interval before any number.
\[P(x) = \frac{\mu^{x} e^{-\mu}}{x!}\]
Then drag the slider on \(\mu\): mean and variance of a Poisson are both \(\mu\), so a high rate gives a wide, bell-shaped pile.

def poisson_steps(rate, hours):
    mu = rate * hours
    print(f"μ = {rate} an hour × {hours:g} hour(s) = {mu:g}")
    P0 = math.exp(-mu)
    print(f"  P(0)  = {mu:g}^0 e^−{mu:g} / 0! = e^−{mu:g} = {P0:.3f}")
    print(f"  P(≥1) = 1 − {P0:.3f} = {1 - P0:.3f}")
    print(f"  P(2)  = {mu:g}² e^−{mu:g} / 2! = {mu**2:g} × {P0:.4f} / 2 = {stats.poisson.pmf(2, mu):.3f}")
    return mu, P0

print("The half hour she is away — rescale first:"); mu_half, P0_half = poisson_steps(3, 0.5)
print("\nA full hour:"); mu_h, P0_h = poisson_steps(3, 1)
print(f"\nWithout the rescaling you would say {P0_h:.0%} for the half hour. It is {P0_half:.0%}: four times out. μ first, always.")
print(f"Reading: leaving the helpline for half an hour, we miss at least one call {1 - P0_half:.0%} of the time — three times out of four.")

The half hour she is away — rescale first:
μ = 3 an hour × 0.5 hour(s) = 1.5
  P(0)  = 1.5^0 e^−1.5 / 0! = e^−1.5 = 0.223
  P(≥1) = 1 − 0.223 = 0.777
  P(2)  = 1.5² e^−1.5 / 2! = 2.25 × 0.2231 / 2 = 0.251

A full hour:
μ = 3 an hour × 1 hour(s) = 3
  P(0)  = 3^0 e^−3 / 0! = e^−3 = 0.050
  P(≥1) = 1 − 0.050 = 0.950
  P(2)  = 3² e^−3 / 2! = 9 × 0.0498 / 2 = 0.224

Without the rescaling you would say 5% for the half hour. It is 22%: four times out. μ first, always.
Reading: leaving the helpline for half an hour, we miss at least one call 78% of the time — three times out of four.



mus = np.round(np.arange(0.5, 10.01, 0.5), 1)
xs = np.arange(0, 21)
fig = go.Figure()
for m in mus:
    fig.add_bar(x=xs, y=stats.poisson.pmf(xs, m), marker_color=RED, visible=bool(m == 1.5), name=f"μ={m}", showlegend=False)
steps = [dict(method="update", label=f"{m:g}", args=[{"visible": [j == i for j in range(len(mus))]},
         {"title": f"μ = {m:g} expected calls → P(0) = {math.exp(-m):.3f}, P(≥1) = {1 - math.exp(-m):.3f}"}]) for i, m in enumerate(mus)]
fig.update_layout(template="simple_white", height=460, title="μ = 1.5 expected calls → P(0) = 0.223, P(≥1) = 0.777",
                  xaxis_title="calls in the interval", yaxis_title="probability",
                  sliders=[dict(active=int(np.where(mus == 1.5)[0][0]), steps=steps, currentvalue=dict(prefix="μ = rate × interval: "))])
fig.show()
print("Half an hour is μ = 1.5, a full hour μ = 3. Push μ to 10 and look: with a high rate the Poisson is a bell too.")

🔍 CHECK
Say which model in words before any formula: how many of these \(n\)? is binomial, you are given \(n\) and \(p\); how many in this interval? is Poisson, you are given a rate and \(\mu\) comes first. \(P(0) + P(\geq 1) = 1\). If your \(P(x)\) is above 1 or your mean is outside \(0..n\), a step is wrong.

title: MBA03 · Week 7 — Three shapes, and how to decide with them
section: B. What range do we promise? — the normal, skewness and kurtosis
text:
B. What range do we promise? — the normal, skewness and kurtosis
Engineering measured 200 bikes on the same loop: 90 km on average, standard deviation 8 km, bell-shaped. \(X \sim N(90, 8)\). Marketing wants to print 75 km.
\[z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\]
Four steps, every time: sketch and shade → standardise → table → sentence. The table gives the area to the left of \(z\); one table serves every bell, because step 2 turns every bell into the same one. Backwards, for a guarantee: area \(\to z \to x = \mu + z\sigma\), and the answer ends in km.
Below the steps, three sliders, one at a time from the baseline \(N(90, 8)\), threshold 75: the mean \(\mu\), the spread \(\sigma\), and the threshold printed on the box. The shaded tail is the share of riders who see less than promised.

def table_left(z):
    # what the printed standard normal table shows: z to two decimals, area to the left to four
    return round(stats.norm.cdf(round(z, 2)), 4)

def normal_steps(x, mu, sigma, tail="below"):
    z = (x - mu) / sigma
    z2 = round(z, 2)                                       # the table has two decimals
    left = table_left(z)
    print(f"1. sketch: the bell centred at {mu}, shade the area {tail} {x}")
    print(f"2. standardise: z = ({x} − {mu}) / {sigma} = {x - mu} / {sigma} = {z:.3f} ≈ {z2:.2f}")
    print(f"3. table, area to the left of {z2:.2f}: {left:.4f}   (Excel: =NORM.S.DIST({z2:.2f}, TRUE))")
    area = left if tail == "below" else 1 - left
    if tail == "above":
        print(f"   the whole area is 1, so P(X > {x}) = 1 − {left:.4f} = {area:.3f}")
    print(f"4. P(X {'<' if tail == 'below' else '>'} {x}) = {area:.3f}")
    return z, area

print("Print 75 km: what share of riders see less?"); z75, below75 = normal_steps(75, 90, 8)
print(f"   Sentence: print 75 km and about {round(below75*100):.0f} riders in a hundred will see less than the box promised.\n")
print("And the share above 75 km:"); _, above75 = normal_steps(75, 90, 8, tail="above")

print("\nBackwards — the Board accepts 5% below the box. What do we print?")
z05 = -1.645                                                # .05 sits between z = −1.64 (.0505) and −1.65 (.0495)
x05 = 90 + z05 * 8
print(f"   table, backwards: area .05 → z = {z05}   (Excel: =NORM.S.INV(0.05) = {stats.norm.ppf(.05):.3f})")
print(f"   undo the standardisation: x = μ + zσ = 90 + ({z05}) × 8 = 90 − {abs(z05)*8:.1f} = {x05:.1f} km")
print(f"   Print 76 km, a promise rounds down: the share below it is P(z < {(76-90)/8:.2f}) = {table_left((76-90)/8):.3f}.")
print("   Sentence: print 76 km; about one rider in twenty-five will see less, and every km added to the box adds one or two complaints in a hundred.")

Print 75 km: what share of riders see less?
1. sketch: the bell centred at 90, shade the area below 75
2. standardise: z = (75 − 90) / 8 = -15 / 8 = -1.875 ≈ -1.88
3. table, area to the left of -1.88: 0.0301   (Excel: =NORM.S.DIST(-1.88, TRUE))
4. P(X < 75) = 0.030
   Sentence: print 75 km and about 3 riders in a hundred will see less than the box promised.

And the share above 75 km:
1. sketch: the bell centred at 90, shade the area above 75
2. standardise: z = (75 − 90) / 8 = -15 / 8 = -1.875 ≈ -1.88
3. table, area to the left of -1.88: 0.0301   (Excel: =NORM.S.DIST(-1.88, TRUE))
   the whole area is 1, so P(X > 75) = 1 − 0.0301 = 0.970
4. P(X > 75) = 0.970

Backwards — the Board accepts 5% below the box. What do we print?
   table, backwards: area .05 → z = -1.645   (Excel: =NORM.S.INV(0.05) = -1.645)
   undo the standardisation: x = μ + zσ = 90 + (-1.645) × 8 = 90 − 13.2 = 76.8 km
   Print 76 km, a promise rounds down: the share below it is P(z < -1.75) = 0.040.
   Sentence: print 76 km; about one rider in twenty-five will see less, and every km added to the box adds one or two complaints in a hundred.



mus_ = list(range(80, 101, 2)); sigmas_ = list(range(4, 17, 2)); thr_ = list(range(70, 91, 1))
grid = np.linspace(50, 130, 400)

def bell(mu, sigma, thr, visible):
    pdf = stats.norm.pdf(grid, mu, sigma); tail = grid <= thr
    return [go.Scatter(x=grid, y=pdf, mode="lines", line=dict(color=INK, width=3), visible=visible, showlegend=False),
            go.Scatter(x=grid[tail], y=pdf[tail], fill="tozeroy", mode="lines", line=dict(color=RED, width=0),
                       fillcolor="rgba(175,31,37,.45)", visible=visible, showlegend=False)]
settings = [(m, 8, 75) for m in mus_] + [(90, s, 75) for s in sigmas_] + [(90, 8, t) for t in thr_]
fig = go.Figure()
for (m, s, t) in settings:
    fig.add_traces(bell(m, s, t, (m, s, t) == (90, 8, 75)))
T = 2 * len(settings)
def vis(idx):
    v = [False] * T; v[2*idx] = v[2*idx + 1] = True; return v
def title(m, s, t):
    return f"N({m}, {s}), box says {t} km → z = {(t-m)/s:.2f}, share below = {stats.norm.cdf(t, m, s):.3f}"
mk = lambda i, lab: dict(method="update", label=lab, args=[{"visible": vis(i)}, {"title": title(*settings[i])}])
off = 0; steps_mu = [mk(off + i, str(m)) for i, m in enumerate(mus_)]
off += len(mus_); steps_sg = [mk(off + i, str(s)) for i, s in enumerate(sigmas_)]
off += len(sigmas_); steps_th = [mk(off + i, str(t)) for i, t in enumerate(thr_)]
fig.update_layout(template="simple_white", height=600, title=title(90, 8, 75), xaxis_title="range, km", yaxis_title="density",
                  yaxis_range=[0, 0.105], margin=dict(b=260),
                  sliders=[dict(active=mus_.index(90), steps=steps_mu, currentvalue=dict(prefix="μ (σ = 8, box 75): "), y=-0.04),
                           dict(active=sigmas_.index(8), steps=steps_sg, currentvalue=dict(prefix="σ (μ = 90, box 75): "), y=-0.30),
                           dict(active=thr_.index(75), steps=steps_th, currentvalue=dict(prefix="box says, km (μ = 90, σ = 8): "), y=-0.56)])
fig.show()
print(f"{'print':>8} {'share who see less':>20}")
for t in (85, 80, 76.8, 75):
    print(f"{t:>8} {stats.norm.cdf(t, 90, 8):>20.0%}")
print("\nDouble σ to 16 and the 75-km tail grows from 3% to 17%: the spread, not the mean, is what a guarantee pays for.")

print("The empirical rule — the same three numbers for every bell, which is why we measure distance in σ and not in km\n")
print(f"{'within':>8} {'km range':>12} {'share, exact':>13} {'rule of thumb':>14}")
for k, rule in zip((1, 2, 3), ("68%", "95%", "99.7%")):
    share = stats.norm.cdf(k) - stats.norm.cdf(-k)
    print(f"{k:>7}σ {f'{mu - k*sigma} to {mu + k*sigma}':>12} {share:>13.3f} {rule:>14}")
print(f"\nA bike at 74 km is two σ below the mean: P(z < −2) = {stats.norm.cdf(-2):.3f}, about one in forty.")
print(f"Beyond three σ either side, under the bell: {2*stats.norm.cdf(-3):.4f}, about one in three hundred — remember this number for kurtosis.")

The empirical rule — the same three numbers for every bell, which is why we measure distance in σ and not in km

  within     km range  share, exact  rule of thumb
      1σ     82 to 98         0.683            68%
      2σ    74 to 106         0.954            95%
      3σ    66 to 114         0.997          99.7%

A bike at 74 km is two σ below the mean: P(z < −2) = 0.023, about one in forty.
Beyond three σ either side, under the bell: 0.0027, about one in three hundred — remember this number for kurtosis.



Skewness and kurtosis: when the bell is the wrong picture
Battery range is symmetric: mean and median coincide, skewness zero. Delivery time is not — most parcels take two days, a few take ten: a long right tail pulls the mean above the median, positive skewness. And kurtosis asks how much of the curve sits in the tails: with the same mean and σ, a fat-tailed shape has a “three σ” day far more often than one in three hundred.
Below, three simulated samples of 5,000 with the same mean and σ: a bell, a right-skewed lognormal, a fat-tailed \(t\). Before you use the table, ask whether the data are a bell.

rng = np.random.default_rng(16)
N_ = 5000
def rescale(x, mu=90, sd=8):                       # same mean and σ for all three, so only the shape differs
    return mu + (x - x.mean()) / x.std() * sd
bell_s   = rescale(rng.normal(size=N_))                 # symmetric: battery range
skewed_s = rescale(rng.lognormal(0, .7, size=N_))       # right-skewed: delivery time, rescaled
fat_s    = rescale(rng.standard_t(3, size=N_))          # fat tails: delivery delays, rescaled

fig = go.Figure()
for name, x, col in (("bell (battery range)", bell_s, GREY), ("right-skewed (lognormal)", skewed_s, RED), ("fat-tailed (t, 3 d.f.)", fat_s, GOLD)):
    fig.add_histogram(x=x, xbins=dict(start=50, end=130, size=1), name=name, marker_color=col, opacity=.6)
fig.update_layout(template="simple_white", height=440, barmode="overlay", title="Three shapes, the same mean 90 and the same σ 8",
                  xaxis_title="value", yaxis_title="count of 5,000", xaxis_range=[50, 130], legend=dict(x=.62, y=.95))
fig.show()

print(f"{'sample':<26} {'mean':>6} {'median':>7} {'skewness':>9} {'kurtosis':>9} {'beyond 3σ':>10}   in plain words")
for name, x in (("bell", bell_s), ("right-skewed lognormal", skewed_s), ("fat-tailed t", fat_s)):
    sk, ku = stats.skew(x), stats.kurtosis(x)         # scipy's kurtosis is excess kurtosis: 0 for the bell
    far = np.mean(np.abs(x - 90) > 24)
    words = ("mean ≈ median, tails like the bell: the table applies" if abs(sk) < .2 and abs(ku) < .5 else
             "mean > median: leans right, a z from the mean gives the wrong areas" if sk > .5 else
             "symmetric but fat tails: the rare bad day is not as rare as the bell says")
    print(f"{name:<26} {x.mean():>6.1f} {np.median(x):>7.1f} {sk:>+9.2f} {ku:>+9.2f} {far:>10.4f}   {words}")
print("\nSkewness: zero for a bell, positive when the long tail is on the right. Kurtosis (excess): zero for a bell, positive for fat tails.")
print("Under the bell, 'beyond three σ' is about .003; the fat-tailed sample has several times that with the same σ.")

The table only gives “to the left”. Everything else is \(1 -\) or a difference of two lookups; the sketch tells you which. Forwards: \(x \to z \to\) area. Backwards: area \(\to z \to x\), and the answer ends in km, not in \(z\). And before any of it: mean above median says the data lean; fat tails say the bell under-counts the surprises.

title: MBA03 · Week 7 — Three shapes, and how to decide with them
section: C. Which supplier do we sign? — expected value to decide
text:
C. Which supplier do we sign? — expected value to decide
Arno Bikes buys 1,000 batteries a month. Volta: €180 a battery, faulty ones replaced by Volta — a certain number. Ampere: €165 a battery, but 5% arrive faulty and a faulty battery costs us €90 to swap on the line — a random variable, Thursday’s table with two rows.
\[E(x) = \sum x\,P(x) \qquad \sigma^{2} = \sum (x - \mu)^{2}\,P(x)\]
Business reading: a cheaper price with a catch is not a price; it is a distribution, and you compare distributions by their mean — and then by their spread. The decision tree: a square where we choose, a circle where chance chooses; the number at a node is the expected value of everything to its right.

def rv_table(values, shares, unit="€"):
    v, P = np.array(values, dtype=float), np.array(shares, dtype=float)
    assert abs(P.sum() - 1) < 1e-9, "shares must add to 1"
    mu = (v * P).sum()
    t = pd.DataFrame({"x": v, "P(x)": P, "x·P(x)": v * P, "x − μ": v - mu, "(x − μ)²": (v - mu) ** 2,
                      "(x − μ)²·P(x)": (v - mu) ** 2 * P})
    t.loc["sum"] = ["", P.sum(), mu, "", "", ((v - mu) ** 2 * P).sum()]
    print(t.to_string(index=False))
    var = ((v - mu) ** 2 * P).sum()
    print(f"\nE(x) = {' + '.join(f'{b:.2f} × {a:g}' for a, b in zip(v, P))} = {' + '.join(f'{a*b:.2f}' for a, b in zip(v, P))} = {unit}{mu:.2f}")
    print(f"σ² = {var:.2f},  σ = √{var:.2f} = {unit}{math.sqrt(var):.1f}")
    return mu, var

print("Ampere, cost per battery — the chance node:\n")
E_amp, V_amp = rv_table([165, 165 + 90], [.95, .05])
sd_amp = math.sqrt(V_amp)
print(f"\nOn average Ampere costs €{E_amp:.2f} a battery: the €165 price plus €{.05*90:.2f} for the faulty ones.")
print(f"Against Volta's €180: €{180 - E_amp:.2f} cheaper a battery, €{1000*(180 - E_amp):,.0f} a month.\n")

tree = pd.DataFrame({"Volta": ["€180.00", "€0", "€180"], "Ampere": [f"€{E_amp:.2f}", f"€{sd_amp:.1f}", "€255"]},
                    index=["expected cost", "spread σ", "worst battery"])
print(tree.to_string())
print("\nExpected value picks Ampere. Spread picks Volta. A decision has two numbers, and the Board must hear both.")

Ampere, cost per battery — the chance node:

     x  P(x)  x·P(x) x − μ (x − μ)²  (x − μ)²·P(x)
 165.0  0.95  156.75  -4.5    20.25        19.2375
 255.0  0.05   12.75  85.5  7310.25       365.5125
        1.00  169.50                      384.7500

E(x) = 0.95 × 165 + 0.05 × 255 = 156.75 + 12.75 = €169.50
σ² = 384.75,  σ = √384.75 = €19.6

On average Ampere costs €169.50 a battery: the €165 price plus €4.50 for the faulty ones.
Against Volta's €180: €10.50 cheaper a battery, €10,500 a month.

                 Volta   Ampere
expected cost  €180.00  €169.50
spread σ            €0    €19.6
worst battery     €180     €255

Expected value picks Ampere. Spread picks Volta. A decision has two numbers, and the Board must hear both.



# When does the spread matter? Volume.
n_m, p_f = 1000, .05
mu_f, sd_f = n_m * p_f, math.sqrt(n_m * p_f * (1 - p_f))
print(f"A thousand batteries a month — the faulty count is binomial, n = {n_m}, p = {p_f}:")
print(f"  np = {mu_f:.0f} faulty,  σ = √({n_m} × {p_f} × {1-p_f}) = {sd_f:.1f}")
bill, bill_sd = 165 * n_m + 90 * mu_f, 90 * sd_f
print(f"  monthly bill = €165 × {n_m:,} + €90 × {mu_f:.0f} = €{bill:,.0f}, give or take €{bill_sd:,.0f}. The €{1000*(180-E_amp):,.0f} saving is never at risk.\n")

n_r = 10
saving_r = n_r * (180 - 165)
P0_r, P1_r = stats.binom.pmf(0, n_r, p_f), stats.binom.pmf(1, n_r, p_f)
P2plus = 1 - P0_r - P1_r
print(f"A rush order of ten — same p, n = {n_r}: the saving on ten batteries is €{saving_r}; two faulty cost €{2*90} and wipe it out.")
print(f"  P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(0) − P(1) = 1 − {P0_r:.3f} − {P1_r:.3f} = {P2plus:.3f}   — one rush order in {round(1/P2plus)}.")
print("\nBoard sentence: sign Ampere for the volume contract, €10.50 a battery cheaper on average and the faults average out to about fifty,")
print("give or take seven. Keep Volta for rush orders of a few units, where one faulty battery in a box of ten is a problem the saving cannot pay for.")
print("Expected value decides when the decision repeats. Spread decides when it does not.")

A thousand batteries a month — the faulty count is binomial, n = 1000, p = 0.05:
  np = 50 faulty,  σ = √(1000 × 0.05 × 0.95) = 6.9
  monthly bill = €165 × 1,000 + €90 × 50 = €169,500, give or take €620. The €10,500 saving is never at risk.

A rush order of ten — same p, n = 10: the saving on ten batteries is €150; two faulty cost €180 and wipe it out.
  P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(0) − P(1) = 1 − 0.599 − 0.315 = 0.086   — one rush order in 12.

Board sentence: sign Ampere for the volume contract, €10.50 a battery cheaper on average and the faults average out to about fifty,
give or take seven. Keep Volta for rush orders of a few units, where one faulty battery in a box of ten is a problem the saving cannot pay for.
Expected value decides when the decision repeats. Spread decides when it does not.



# Drag Ampere's defect rate: when does the expected value flip back to Volta?
rates = np.round(np.arange(0.00, 0.3001, 0.01), 2)
def ev_amp(r, price=165, swap=90):
    return price + r * swap
flip = (180 - 165) / 90                      # the rate at which 165 + r × 90 = 180
fig = go.Figure()
for r in rates:
    e = ev_amp(r); sd = math.sqrt((1 - r) * (165 - e) ** 2 + r * (255 - e) ** 2)
    fig.add_bar(x=["Volta", "Ampere"], y=[180, e], marker_color=[GREY, RED if e < 180 else INK], visible=bool(abs(r - .05) < 1e-9),
                text=["€180.00", f"€{e:.2f} ± {sd:.1f}"], textposition="outside", showlegend=False, name=f"{r:.0%}")
fig.add_hline(y=180, line=dict(color=GOLD, dash="dot"), annotation_text="Volta, certain €180")
steps = [dict(method="update", label=f"{r:.0%}",
              args=[{"visible": [j == i for j in range(len(rates))]},
                    {"title": f"Ampere defect rate {r:.0%} → expected cost €{ev_amp(r):.2f} a battery  ({'Ampere cheaper' if ev_amp(r) < 180 else 'Volta cheaper' if ev_amp(r) > 180 else 'a tie'})"}])
         for i, r in enumerate(rates)]
fig.update_layout(template="simple_white", height=460, yaxis_range=[150, 215], yaxis_title="expected cost per battery, €",
                  title="Ampere defect rate 5% → expected cost €169.50 a battery  (Ampere cheaper)",
                  sliders=[dict(active=int(np.argmin(abs(rates - .05))), steps=steps, currentvalue=dict(prefix="Ampere's defect rate: "))])
fig.show()
print(f"{'defect rate':>12} {'E(Ampere)':>10} {'vs Volta':>10}")
for r in (.00, .05, .10, flip, .20):
    print(f"{r:>12.1%} {ev_amp(r):>10.2f} {ev_amp(r) - 180:>+10.2f}")
print(f"\nThe expected value flips at a defect rate of 15/90 = {flip:.1%}: above that, the €15 discount no longer pays for the swaps.")

🔍 CHECK
Shares at the chance node add to 1; the worst end node is the price plus the full cost of the catch. The expected value is the price you pay on average; the spread is the surprise you pay sometimes. A repeated decision follows the mean; a one-off weighs the spread. If your \(E(x)\) is below the best end node or above the worst, the weights are wrong.

title: MBA03 · Week 7 — Three shapes, and how to decide with them
section: D. How many late orders in 250? — the normal approximation, then Monte Carlo
text:
D. How many late orders in 250? — the normal approximation, then Monte Carlo
Each of 250 orders ships late with \(p = .06\), alone: binomial. The logistics partner charges a penalty when a month has 20 or more late orders. The four steps of block A would need \(\binom{250}{20}\) and \(.94^{230}\), then the same for 21, 22, … 250: nobody does that by hand.
\[\mu = np \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{np(1-p)} \qquad z = \frac{x - \tfrac{1}{2} - \mu}{\sigma}\]
Business reading: with many trials the bars become a bell, so a count is read like a measurement: \(np\), \(\sqrt{np(1-p)}\), then block B’s four steps. It works when \(np \geq 5\) and \(n(1-p) \geq 5\). A bar for a whole number spans half a unit each side, so “20 or more” starts at 19.5: the half unit, or continuity correction.

n, p = 250, .06
mu_n, sd_n = n * p, math.sqrt(n * p * (1 - p))
print(f"μ = np = {n} × {p} = {mu_n:g} late orders")
print(f"σ = √np(1−p) = √({n} × {p} × {1-p}) = √{n*p*(1-p):.1f} = {sd_n:.3f}")
print(f"check: np = {mu_n:g} ≥ 5 and n(1−p) = {n*(1-p):g} ≥ 5 → the bell may be used\n")

print("Twenty or more late, with the half unit:")
z_half, P_half = normal_steps(19.5, mu_n, round(sd_n, 3), tail="above")
exact = 1 - stats.binom.cdf(19, n, p)
print(f"\nThe exact binomial, summed by a computer: P(X ≥ 20) = {exact:.3f} — the bell is off by three in a thousand.")
z_no = (20 - mu_n) / sd_n
print(f"Without the half unit: z = 5 / {sd_n:.3f} = {z_no:.2f}, area {1 - table_left(z_no):.3f} — a tenth too small. Use the half unit, and move on.")
print(f"\nSentence: of 250 orders, expect 15 late, give or take four. A penalty month comes about one month in {round(1/P_half)}.")
print(f"Cut the late rate to 4% and P(X ≥ 20) = {1 - stats.binom.cdf(19, 250, .04):.3f}: rarer than one in fifty.")

μ = np = 250 × 0.06 = 15 late orders
σ = √np(1−p) = √(250 × 0.06 × 0.94) = √14.1 = 3.755
check: np = 15 ≥ 5 and n(1−p) = 235 ≥ 5 → the bell may be used

Twenty or more late, with the half unit:
1. sketch: the bell centred at 15.0, shade the area above 19.5
2. standardise: z = (19.5 − 15.0) / 3.755 = 4.5 / 3.755 = 1.198 ≈ 1.20
3. table, area to the left of 1.20: 0.8849   (Excel: =NORM.S.DIST(1.20, TRUE))
   the whole area is 1, so P(X > 19.5) = 1 − 0.8849 = 0.115
4. P(X > 19.5) = 0.115

The exact binomial, summed by a computer: P(X ≥ 20) = 0.118 — the bell is off by three in a thousand.
Without the half unit: z = 5 / 3.755 = 1.33, area 0.092 — a tenth too small. Use the half unit, and move on.

Sentence: of 250 orders, expect 15 late, give or take four. A penalty month comes about one month in 9.
Cut the late rate to 4% and P(X ≥ 20) = 0.003: rarer than one in fifty.



xs = np.arange(0, 36)
pmf = stats.binom.pmf(xs, n, p)
grid = np.linspace(0, 35, 500)
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_bar(x=xs, y=pmf, marker_color=[RED if x >= 20 else GREY for x in xs], name="exact binomial, n = 250, p = .06", opacity=.85)
fig.add_scatter(x=grid, y=stats.norm.pdf(grid, mu_n, sd_n), mode="lines", line=dict(color=INK, width=3), name=f"N(15, {sd_n:.3f})")
tail = grid >= 19.5
fig.add_scatter(x=grid[tail], y=stats.norm.pdf(grid[tail], mu_n, sd_n), fill="tozeroy", mode="lines", line=dict(width=0),
                fillcolor="rgba(175,31,37,.3)", name="area from 19.5: the bell's P(X ≥ 20)")
fig.add_vline(x=19.5, line=dict(color=GOLD, width=2, dash="dash"), annotation_text="19.5, the half unit", annotation_position="top right")
fig.update_layout(template="simple_white", height=460, title="The bars become a bell: late orders among 250",
                  xaxis_title="late orders in the month", yaxis_title="probability", legend=dict(x=.55, y=.95))
fig.show()
print(f"red bars (exact) = {pmf[xs >= 20].sum():.3f}    shaded area from 19.5 (bell) = {1 - stats.norm.cdf(19.5, mu_n, sd_n):.3f}    without the half unit, from 20 = {1 - stats.norm.cdf(20, mu_n, sd_n):.3f}")

Unable to display output for mime type(s): application/vnd.plotly.v1+json


red bars (exact) = 0.118    shaded area from 19.5 (bell) = 0.115    without the half unit, from 20 = 0.092



Monte Carlo: when you cannot compute, simulate
Twelve test rides, \(p = .25\). Instead of the formula, play the Saturday: twelve coin flips, each lands “buy” one time in four, count the buyers. Then play a thousand Saturdays and let the counts pile into bars. The histogram of the simulation is the binomial: the formula is the shortcut, the simulation is the thing itself — and it still runs when there is no formula (two couriers, a rate that changes with the weather, faults that come in batches).

rng = np.random.default_rng(83)
S = 1000
saturdays = rng.random((S, 12)) < .25            # 1,000 Saturdays × 12 riders: True = buys
buyers = saturdays.sum(axis=1)
print("The first five Saturdays, played:", ", ".join(f"{b} buyer{'s' if b != 1 else ''}" for b in buyers[:5]))

xs = np.arange(0, 13)
counts = np.bincount(buyers, minlength=13)
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_bar(x=xs, y=counts / S, marker_color=RED, name="1,000 simulated Saturdays", opacity=.85)
fig.add_scatter(x=xs, y=stats.binom.pmf(xs, 12, .25), mode="markers+lines", marker=dict(color=INK, size=9), line=dict(color=INK, dash="dot"),
                name="binomial formula, n = 12, p = .25")
fig.update_layout(template="simple_white", height=440, title="A thousand Saturdays, counted — and the formula on top",
                  xaxis_title="buyers out of 12", yaxis_title="share of Saturdays", legend=dict(x=.55, y=.95))
fig.show()

with3, with0 = int(counts[3]), int(counts[0])
print(f"Saturdays with exactly 3 buyers: {with3} of 1,000 ({with3/S:.3f}); the formula says {stats.binom.pmf(3, 12, .25):.3f}, about {1000*stats.binom.pmf(3, 12, .25):.0f}")
print(f"Saturdays with none:             {with0} of 1,000 ({with0/S:.3f}); the formula says {stats.binom.pmf(0, 12, .25):.3f}, about {1000*stats.binom.pmf(0, 12, .25):.0f}")
print(f"mean buyers {buyers.mean():.2f} vs np = 3;  sd {buyers.std():.2f} vs √np(1−p) = 1.5.  Not exactly: a thousand is a sample too.")

The first five Saturdays, played: 2 buyers, 2 buyers, 3 buyers, 5 buyers, 1 buyer


Unable to display output for mime type(s): application/vnd.plotly.v1+json


Saturdays with exactly 3 buyers: 257 of 1,000 (0.257); the formula says 0.258, about 258
Saturdays with none:             29 of 1,000 (0.029); the formula says 0.032, about 32
mean buyers 2.98 vs np = 3;  sd 1.50 vs √np(1−p) = 1.5.  Not exactly: a thousand is a sample too.



# Same trick for the 250 orders: play the month a thousand times
months = (rng.random((S, 250)) < .06).sum(axis=1)
late20 = int((months >= 20).sum())
print(f"Months with 20 or more late orders: {late20} of 1,000 ({late20/S:.3f})")
print(f"  the exact binomial says {1 - stats.binom.cdf(19, 250, .06):.3f}, about {1000*(1 - stats.binom.cdf(19, 250, .06)):.0f}; the bell estimated {1 - stats.norm.cdf(19.5, 15, math.sqrt(14.1)):.3f}")
print(f"  mean late orders {months.mean():.2f} vs np = 15;  sd {months.std():.2f} vs √np(1−p) = {math.sqrt(14.1):.3f}")

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_histogram(x=months, xbins=dict(start=-0.5, end=35.5, size=1), histnorm="probability", marker_color=RED, opacity=.85, name="1,000 simulated months")
fig.add_scatter(x=np.arange(0, 36), y=stats.binom.pmf(np.arange(0, 36), 250, .06), mode="markers+lines", marker=dict(color=INK, size=7),
                line=dict(color=INK, dash="dot"), name="exact binomial")
fig.add_vline(x=19.5, line=dict(color=GOLD, width=2, dash="dash"), annotation_text="penalty from 20", annotation_position="top right")
fig.update_layout(template="simple_white", height=420, title="A thousand months of 250 orders", xaxis_title="late orders", yaxis_title="share of months",
                  legend=dict(x=.6, y=.95))
fig.show()
print("\nThe formula needs the model to be clean: same p, independent trials. A simulation only needs you to describe one month honestly.")

Months with 20 or more late orders: 118 of 1,000 (0.118)
  the exact binomial says 0.118, about 118; the bell estimated 0.115
  mean late orders 15.09 vs np = 15;  sd 3.80 vs √np(1−p) = 3.755


Unable to display output for mime type(s): application/vnd.plotly.v1+json



The formula needs the model to be clean: same p, independent trials. A simulation only needs you to describe one month honestly.




🔍 CHECK
Before the bell: \(np \geq 5\) and \(n(1-p) \geq 5\), both written down. “20 or more” starts at 19.5, “20 or fewer” ends at 20.5; the sketch tells you which side the half unit goes. The simulation must land within a few in a thousand of the formula — if it does not, the model you simulated is not the model you computed.

title: MBA03 · Week 7 — Three shapes, and how to decide with them
section: Drills, solved in code
text:
Drills, solved in code
This section is an optional companion: the code is not examined, but reading it is recommended. Every drill in drills.md is solved here in Python. Do the drill on paper first, then run the cell and compare your numbers with the output.

# `close` checks our result against the number printed in drills.md
def close(value, expected, tol=1e-3):
    assert abs(value - expected) <= tol, f"got {value}, drills.md says {expected}"

print("helpers ready")

helpers ready


D1. (a) Saturday brings 10 test rides; three riders in ten buy, each deciding alone. Name the model; find \(P(2)\), \(P(0)\), \(P(\geq 1)\), the mean and the standard deviation. (b) Web-shop orders arrive at random, 4 an hour: name the model, find \(P(0)\) and \(P(2)\) in an hour; then, for a 15-minute coffee break, \(\mu\) first, \(P(0)\) and \(P(\geq 1)\).

# D1 (a)
n, p = 10, .3
print("(a) Binomial: a fixed number of trials (10), each yes or no, the same p = .3 every time, each rider alone.\n")
P2 = binomial_steps(n, 2, p)
P0 = (1 - p) ** n
print(f"\nP(0) = .7^10 = {P0:.3f}     P(≥1) = 1 − {P0:.3f} = {1 - P0:.3f}")
print(f"np = 10 × .3 = {n*p:g} buyers     σ = √(10 × .3 × .7) = √{n*p*(1-p):.1f} = {math.sqrt(n*p*(1-p)):.2f}")
close(math.comb(10, 2), 45); close(.3 ** 2, .09, 1e-9); close(.7 ** 8, .05765, 1e-4); close(45 * .09 * .05765, .233); close(P2, .233)
close(P0, .028); close(1 - P0, .972); close(n * p, 3); close(n * p * (1 - p), 2.1, 1e-9); close(math.sqrt(n * p * (1 - p)), 1.45)
print("Expect three buyers, give or take one and a half; a Saturday with no sale happens about three times in a hundred.\n")

# D1 (b)
print("(b) Poisson: orders arrive at random over time, at a constant rate, with no ceiling on the count.\n")
print("One hour:"); mu4, P0_4 = poisson_steps(4, 1)
print("\nA 15-minute break — a quarter of an hour, so μ first:"); mu1, P0_1 = poisson_steps(4, 0.25)
close(math.exp(-4), .01832, 1e-4); close(P0_4, .018); close(stats.poisson.pmf(2, 4), .147); close(16 * .01832 / 2, .147)
close(mu1, 1, 1e-9); close(P0_1, .368); close(1 - P0_1, .632)
print("\nA silent hour is rare, two in a hundred; a silent coffee break happens more than once in three.")

(a) Binomial: a fixed number of trials (10), each yes or no, the same p = .3 every time, each rider alone.

1. the ways to pick which 2 of the 10 buy:   C(10,2) = 45
2. those 2 buy:                              0.3^2 = 0.090000
3. the other 8 do not:                      0.7^8 = 0.0576
4. multiply:                                 45 × 0.090000 × 0.0576 = 0.233

P(0) = .7^10 = 0.028     P(≥1) = 1 − 0.028 = 0.972
np = 10 × .3 = 3 buyers     σ = √(10 × .3 × .7) = √2.1 = 1.45
Expect three buyers, give or take one and a half; a Saturday with no sale happens about three times in a hundred.

(b) Poisson: orders arrive at random over time, at a constant rate, with no ceiling on the count.

One hour:
μ = 4 an hour × 1 hour(s) = 4
  P(0)  = 4^0 e^−4 / 0! = e^−4 = 0.018
  P(≥1) = 1 − 0.018 = 0.982
  P(2)  = 4² e^−4 / 2! = 16 × 0.0183 / 2 = 0.147

A 15-minute break — a quarter of an hour, so μ first:
μ = 4 an hour × 0.25 hour(s) = 1
  P(0)  = 1^0 e^−1 / 0! = e^−1 = 0.368
  P(≥1) = 1 − 0.368 = 0.632
  P(2)  = 1² e^−1 / 2! = 1 × 0.3679 / 2 = 0.184

A silent hour is rare, two in a hundred; a silent coffee break happens more than once in three.


D2. Bike weight off the line: \(X \sim N(22,\,1.5)\) kg. (a) Share under 20 kg. (b) Share between 21 and 24 kg. (c) The heaviest 5% are sent back for a check: from what weight? End in kg. (d) Delivery times: mean 3.1 days, median 2.4 — what shape, and why is the table the wrong tool?

mu, sigma = 22, 1.5
print("(a) shade the left tail below 20 kg"); z_a, below20 = normal_steps(20, mu, sigma)
close(z_a, -1.333); close(table_left(z_a), .0918, 1e-4); close(below20, .092)
print("    About nine bikes in a hundred come in under 20 kg; the customer will wait, or pay for the light frame.\n")

print("(b) shade between 21 and 24: two lookups, area to the left of each, and a difference")
z_lo, z_hi = (21 - mu) / sigma, (24 - mu) / sigma
between = table_left(z_hi) - table_left(z_lo)
print(f"    z = {z_lo:.2f} and z = {z_hi:.2f}:  P({z_lo:.2f} < z < {z_hi:.2f}) = {table_left(z_hi):.4f} − {table_left(z_lo):.4f} = {between:.3f}")
close(z_lo, -0.667); close(z_hi, 1.333); close(table_left(z_hi), .9082, 1e-4); close(table_left(z_lo), .2514, 1e-4); close(between, .657)
close(stats.norm.cdf(24, mu, sigma) - stats.norm.cdf(21, mu, sigma), .656)
print("    Two bikes in three weigh between 21 and 24 kg.\n")

print("(c) backwards: the heaviest 5% is the right tail, so 95% of the area is to the left of the threshold")
print(f"    find .9500 inside the table: z = 1.64 gives {table_left(1.64):.4f}, z = 1.65 gives {table_left(1.65):.4f} → z = 1.645   (Excel: =NORM.S.INV(0.95) = {stats.norm.ppf(.95):.3f})")
z_c = 1.645; x_c = mu + z_c * sigma
print(f"    undo the standardisation: x = μ + zσ = 22 + 1.645 × 1.5 = 22 + {z_c*sigma:.2f} = {x_c:.1f} kg")
close(table_left(1.64), .9495, 1e-4); close(table_left(1.65), .9505, 1e-4); close(stats.norm.ppf(.95), 1.645); close(z_c * sigma, 2.47, 5e-3); close(x_c, 24.5, .05)
print("    A bike over about 24.5 kg goes back for a check.\n")

print("(d) delivery times: mean 3.1 days, median 2.4 days")
mean_d, median_d = 3.1, 2.4
assert mean_d > median_d
print(f"    mean − median = {mean_d - median_d:+.1f} days: a long right tail, POSITIVE skewness — most parcels in two or three days, a few much later.")
print("    The normal is symmetric (mean = median), so a z from a mean of 3.1 would give the wrong areas: the table only answers questions about bells.")

(a) shade the left tail below 20 kg
1. sketch: the bell centred at 22, shade the area below 20
2. standardise: z = (20 − 22) / 1.5 = -2 / 1.5 = -1.333 ≈ -1.33
3. table, area to the left of -1.33: 0.0918   (Excel: =NORM.S.DIST(-1.33, TRUE))
4. P(X < 20) = 0.092
    About nine bikes in a hundred come in under 20 kg; the customer will wait, or pay for the light frame.

(b) shade between 21 and 24: two lookups, area to the left of each, and a difference
    z = -0.67 and z = 1.33:  P(-0.67 < z < 1.33) = 0.9082 − 0.2514 = 0.657
    Two bikes in three weigh between 21 and 24 kg.

(c) backwards: the heaviest 5% is the right tail, so 95% of the area is to the left of the threshold
    find .9500 inside the table: z = 1.64 gives 0.9495, z = 1.65 gives 0.9505 → z = 1.645   (Excel: =NORM.S.INV(0.95) = 1.645)
    undo the standardisation: x = μ + zσ = 22 + 1.645 × 1.5 = 22 + 2.47 = 24.5 kg
    A bike over about 24.5 kg goes back for a check.

(d) delivery times: mean 3.1 days, median 2.4 days
    mean − median = +0.7 days: a long right tail, POSITIVE skewness — most parcels in two or three days, a few much later.
    The normal is symmetric (mean = median), so a z from a mean of 3.1 would give the wrong areas: the table only answers questions about bells.


D3. €2,000 for one promotion in December; each extra bike earns the €600 margin (list €1,000, variable cost €400). Test-ride Saturday, cost €2,000: extra sales 6 / 10 / 14 bikes with probability .3 / .5 / .2. Online ads, cost €1,000: extra sales 4 / 6 bikes with probability .5 / .5. (a) The tree with the profit at each end node. (b) Expected profit of each. (c) Standard deviation of each. (d) Two sentences for the Board.

margin = 1000 - 400; close(margin, 600)
sat_x = [b * margin - 2000 for b in (6, 10, 14)]; sat_p = [.3, .5, .2]
ads_x = [b * margin - 1000 for b in (4, 6)];      ads_p = [.5, .5]
print("(a) end-node profits, margin €600 a bike minus the cost of the option")
print("    Saturday (cost €2,000): " + "; ".join(f"{b} × 600 − 2,000 = {x:,}" for b, x in zip((6, 10, 14), sat_x)))
print("    Ads (cost €1,000):      " + "; ".join(f"{b} × 600 − 1,000 = {x:,}" for b, x in zip((4, 6), ads_x)))
assert sat_x == [1600, 4000, 6400] and ads_x == [1400, 2600]
print("    The tree: a square 'which promotion?', two branches; on each a circle with branches .3 / .5 / .2 and .5 / .5, the profits at the ends.\n")

print("(b), (c) Test-ride Saturday:"); E_sat, V_sat = rv_table(sat_x, sat_p)
print("\n(b), (c) Online ads:"); E_ads, V_ads = rv_table(ads_x, ads_p)
assert np.allclose(np.array(sat_x) * sat_p, [480, 2000, 1280]) and np.allclose(np.array(ads_x) * ads_p, [700, 1300])
assert np.allclose(np.array(sat_x) - E_sat, [-2160, 240, 2640]) and np.allclose((np.array(sat_x) - E_sat) ** 2 * sat_p, [1399680, 28800, 1393920])
close(E_sat, 3760, 1e-6); close(E_ads, 2000, 1e-6); close(E_sat - E_ads, 1760, 1e-6)
close(V_sat, 2822400, 1e-6); close(math.sqrt(V_sat), 1680, 1e-6); close(V_ads, 360000, 1e-6); close(math.sqrt(V_ads), 600, 1e-6)
close(1680 / 600, 2.8, 1e-9); assert min(sat_x) == 1600 < E_ads

print(f"\n(d) The test-ride Saturday earns €{E_sat:,.0f} on average against €{E_ads:,.0f} for the ads, €{E_sat - E_ads:,.0f} more; its worst case, €{min(sat_x):,},")
print(f"    still beats the ads' average. Its spread is nearly three times larger (€{math.sqrt(V_sat):,.0f} against €{math.sqrt(V_ads):,.0f}): the Saturday can end anywhere")
print("    between €1,600 and €6,400, the ads between €1,400 and €2,600. Expected value picks the Saturday; the spread says the result will be a")
print("    surprise either way — and since even the bad Saturday beats the ads, the Board can take the Saturday without fear.")

(a) end-node profits, margin €600 a bike minus the cost of the option
    Saturday (cost €2,000): 6 × 600 − 2,000 = 1,600; 10 × 600 − 2,000 = 4,000; 14 × 600 − 2,000 = 6,400
    Ads (cost €1,000):      4 × 600 − 1,000 = 1,400; 6 × 600 − 1,000 = 2,600
    The tree: a square 'which promotion?', two branches; on each a circle with branches .3 / .5 / .2 and .5 / .5, the profits at the ends.

(b), (c) Test-ride Saturday:
      x  P(x)  x·P(x)   x − μ   (x − μ)²  (x − μ)²·P(x)
 1600.0   0.3   480.0 -2160.0  4665600.0      1399680.0
 4000.0   0.5  2000.0   240.0    57600.0        28800.0
 6400.0   0.2  1280.0  2640.0  6969600.0      1393920.0
          1.0  3760.0                         2822400.0

E(x) = 0.30 × 1600 + 0.50 × 4000 + 0.20 × 6400 = 480.00 + 2000.00 + 1280.00 = €3760.00
σ² = 2822400.00,  σ = √2822400.00 = €1680.0

(b), (c) Online ads:
      x  P(x)  x·P(x)  x − μ  (x − μ)²  (x − μ)²·P(x)
 1400.0   0.5   700.0 -600.0  360000.0       180000.0
 2600.0   0.5  1300.0  600.0  360000.0       180000.0
          1.0  2000.0                        360000.0

E(x) = 0.50 × 1400 + 0.50 × 2600 = 700.00 + 1300.00 = €2000.00
σ² = 360000.00,  σ = √360000.00 = €600.0

(d) The test-ride Saturday earns €3,760 on average against €2,000 for the ads, €1,760 more; its worst case, €1,600,
    still beats the ads' average. Its spread is nearly three times larger (€1,680 against €600): the Saturday can end anywhere

Domain is the first question, always: for which q does this mean anything?
\begin{aligned}

section: Nothing here is memorised. Each rule is a question with no answer.
text:
Nothing here is memorised. Each rule is a question with no answer.
Ask what the symbol is asking for, and the restriction falls out on its own.








the symbol
the question it asks
when there is no answer




\sqrt{x}
what number, times itself, gives x?
x < 0 — a square is never negative


\ln x
to what power must e be raised to give x?
x ≤ 0 — a positive base never reaches zero


\dfrac{a}{x}
how many x fit into a?
x = 0 — nothing fits into nothing




So \sqrt{q-20} needs the thing inside, not q, to be at least zero: q − 20 ≥ 0.
Three rules, or one habit: put the bracket’s contents where the rule’s own question can be asked. You will never have to remember which is ≥ and which is > — √0 = 0 is fine, ln 0 is not.

title: The tool that finds the top of any hill
section: Where do you take a limit? Where the domain stops.
text:
Where do you take a limit? Where the domain stops.
Inside the domain there is nothing to ask: substitute and read the value. A limit is for the edges — the places you cannot reach.








the domain stops…
example
the limit to take




at a point that is excluded
\dfrac{120}{q-40}, q \neq 40
from both sides: q \to 40^{-} and q \to 40^{+}


at an open end
AC(q), q > 0
from the allowed side only: q \to 0^{+}


never — it runs on
AC(q), q > 0
q \to +\infty (and -\infty if the domain goes there)



Recipe: write the domain → list its edges → one limit per edge. AC has domain (0, +\infty): two edges, two limits.

title: The tool that finds the top of any hill
section: Which is two limits, and a floor
text:
Which is two limits, and a floor
\lim_{q \to 0^{+}} AC(q) = +\infty \qquad\qquad \lim_{q \to \infty} AC(q) = 400
At q = 0 the expression means nothing — you cannot divide by nothing — but you can ask what happens near zero, and the answer is: ruinous. One bike carries the whole rent.
Far out, the shared rent vanishes and average cost settles onto the variable cost. It never goes below €400, because every bike really does need €400 of parts.
Economies of scale, in two limits. And a limit is exactly this: not the value at a point, but the value the function heads towards as you approach it.

title: The tool that finds the top of any hill
section: The one that looks impossible
text:
The one that looks impossible
\lim_{q \to 10} \frac{q^{2} - 100}{q - 10}
Why at 10? Because 10 is outside the domain (the denominator is zero there): an edge, so a limit. Substitute and you get 0/0, which says nothing. So do not substitute first.

\frac{(q-10)(q+10)}{q-10} = q + 10 \;\longrightarrow\; 20







Board sentence


0/0 is not an answer, it is an instruction: factor, cancel, then substitute.

title: The tool that finds the top of any hill
section: 0/0 is a promise: the same factor is hiding top and bottom
text:
0/0 is a promise: the same factor is hiding top and bottom
Added 22 October · not covered in class
If the top and the bottom are both zero at q = a, both contain the factor (q - a). So after factoring, (q - a) must appear in both and cancel. If it does not, the factoring is wrong: go back, do not go on.



Substitute. Is it really 0/0? A number over a number is the answer; a number over 0 is an infinity.
Factor both until (q - a) shows in each. Watch the sign: a - q = -(q - a).
Cancel, then substitute again. If it is still 0/0, there is another (q - a): cancel once more.


\lim_{q \to 3^{+}} \frac{(q-3)^{2}}{3q - q^{2}}
Top and bottom are 0 at 3, so (q - 3) hides in both. The bottom does not show it — until you flip a sign:
3q - q^{2} = q(3 - q) = -q(q-3)
\frac{(q-3)^{2}}{-q(q-3)} = -\frac{q-3}{q} \;\longrightarrow\; -\frac{0}{3} = 0

The check that saves marks: no (q - a) in both after factoring means a mistake, not a hard limit.

title: The tool that finds the top of any hill
section: One more limit at infinity: is there a slant asymptote?
text:
One more limit at infinity: is there a slant asymptote?
Added 22 October · not covered in class
A curve can approach a sloping line, not just a flat one. Two limits decide it:
m = \lim_{q \to \infty} \frac{f(q)}{q}, \qquad b = \lim_{q \to \infty} \big(f(q) - mq\big)
If both are finite numbers, y = mq + b is the slant asymptote. If m is infinite, or m = 0 (then it is the horizontal case), there is none.

none, and no horizontal one either: it rises forever, ever more slowly



A report that writes “no asymptote” should have checked. Saying so in one line — “C(q)/q → ∞, so no slant asymptote” — is what separates a complete study from a good one.

text:
Question 6: is there something inside something?
ln(q + 1) is not ln q. There is a second function hiding inside the first, and the midterm’s revenue function is exactly this shape.
\frac{d}{dq}\,f\big(g(q)\big) \;=\; f'\big(g(q)\big) \cdot g'(q)
Differentiate the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.



\ln(q+1) \;\to\; \frac{1}{q+1}\cdot \underbrace{1}_{\text{inside}'} = \frac{1}{q+1} \ln(3q) \;\to\; \frac{1}{3q}\cdot 3 = \frac{1}{q}

(2q+5)^{4} \;\to\; 4(2q+5)^{3}\cdot 2 = 8(2q+5)^{3} e^{0.12t} \;\to\; e^{0.12t}\cdot 0.12

Why ln(q+1) looked free: the inside is q + 1, whose derivative is 1, so the multiplication does nothing and you never saw it. Change the inside to 3q and it shows up.

title: The tool that finds the top of any hill
section: From the derivative back to the function
text:
From the derivative back to the function
The exam asks this in one direction and the other. Given f', find f.
f'(q) = 6q^{2} - 2q \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(q) = 2q^{3} - q^{2} + c

The c is not decoration. Every function 2q³ − q² + c has the same derivative, so one extra fact pins it down:
f(1) = 4 \;\Rightarrow\; 2 - 1 + c = 4 \;\Rightarrow\; c = 3

title: The tool that finds the top of any hill
section: And it means something
text:
And it means something
Given marginal cost MC(q) = 0.8q + 3, the cost function is
C(q) = 0.4q^{2} + 3q + c
and c = C(0) is the fixed cost — what you pay having produced nothing.
The constant of integration is not a technicality here. It is the rent.

title: The tool that finds the top of any hill
section: Running it backwards has a name: the integral
text:
Running it backwards has a name: the integral
\int f'(q)\,dq \;=\; f(q) + c \qquad \text{read: “the function whose derivative is } f'\text{”}
Every derivative rule, read from right to left:







you know
so, backwards




q^{n} \to n\,q^{n-1}
\displaystyle\int q^{n}\,dq = \frac{q^{n+1}}{n+1} + c \quad (n \neq -1)


\ln q \to \dfrac{1}{q}
\displaystyle\int \frac{1}{q}\,dq = \ln\lvert q\rvert + c


\ln f(q) \to \dfrac{f'(q)}{f(q)} (chain rule)
\displaystyle\int \frac{f'(q)}{f(q)}\,dq = \ln\lvert f(q)\rvert + c


a constant \to 0
\displaystyle\int k\,dq = kq + c


sums, term by term
integrate term by term



Power up by one, divide by the new power. The one power that rule cannot handle, q^{-1}, is exactly the one that becomes a log. And the check is free: differentiate your answer and you must get back what was inside.

section: The exam’s integral: split the fraction first
text:
The exam’s integral: split the fraction first
The final’s calculus question opens with a fraction to integrate. There is no rule for a fraction — so make it stop being one.
\int \frac{3q^{3} + 4q^{2} - 2}{q}\,dq

= \int \Big(3q^{2} + 4q - \frac{2}{q}\Big)\,dq \;=\; q^{3} + 2q^{2} - 2\ln\lvert q\rvert + c







Board sentence


Divide every term by the denominator, then integrate each piece on its own. The 1/q piece is the one that turns into a log.

title: The tool that finds the top of any hill
section: When the top is the derivative of the bottom
text:
When the top is the derivative of the bottom
A log appears whenever the top is the derivative of the bottom — exactly, or up to a constant you can factor out.


\int \frac{1}{q-1}\,dq = \ln|q-1| + c
The bottom differentiates to 1. A shifted log, nothing more.

\int \frac{q}{q^{2}-1}\,dq = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln|q^{2}-1| + c
The bottom differentiates to 2q; the top is q, so put the missing ½ out front.


Before integrating any fraction, ask one question: is the top the derivative of the bottom? If yes, it is a log. If no, divide term by term and use the power rule.
This is the chain rule read backwards, and the final’s calculus question uses it.

Only a number can be moved outside the integral, never an x: \int \frac{1}{x^{2}-1}dx is not a log of x^{2}-1. text:
The definite integral, and what it measures
Put two numbers on the integral sign: evaluate at the top, subtract the value at the bottom. The c cancels, so leave it out.
\int_{0}^{20} (0.8q + 3)\,dq = \Big[0.4q^{2} + 3q\Big]_{0}^{20} = 220
Add up the marginal cost of the first twenty units and you get what those twenty cost, on top of the fixed cost.

And the one worth remembering, on Arno Bikes’ marginal profit from block C:
\int_{100}^{150} \pi'(q)\,dq = \pi(150) - \pi(100) = €10{,}000
The integral of the marginal is the change in the total. That sentence is the whole of integration.

Differentiate to ask what one more does. Integrate to ask what all of them did.

Because money has a cost. Arno Bikes’ money costs it 9% a year — that is its cost of capital. A euro that arrives in a year instead of today is a year in which it could have paid back 9% or earned 9%. Discounting charges each future euro for its wait.

The crossing has a name: IRR

text:
Take home

A nominal rate is not a price until you know how often it compounds. Compare on EAR.
Compounding more often always helps, and always by less. The ceiling is e.
Money with different dates cannot be added. Bring each sum to today by dividing by (1+r)^t — compounding run backwards.
A firm growing for ever is worth CF_1/(r-g); the gap r-g is where the valuation’s risk sits.
NPV = every flow brought to today, outlay included, added up. Accept when it is positive at your own cost of capital; IRR is the rate where it crosses zero.
The cost of capital is the WACC: what shareholders and lenders want, weighted by their share of the money, with the tax saving on interest.

Combinations: a team of three, order does not matter


Eight people work at Arno Bikes. The founder sends three to the Milan trade fair.







Bet before we compute


How many different teams of three? More or fewer than 100?




A team is a team: Anna, Luca, Sara is the same team as Sara, Anna, Luca.


\binom{8}{3} = \frac{8!}{3!\,(8-3)!}

\binom{8}{3} reads “8 choose 3”: the number of groups of 3 you can pick from 8.
n! reads “n factorial”: n \cdot (n-1) \cdot (n-2) \cdots 1, the ways to line up n people. 3! = 6, 8! = 40{,}320.



Never compute the big factorials. Cancel first:
\frac{8!}{3!\,5!} = \frac{8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot \cancel{5!}}{3! \cdot \cancel{5!}} = \frac{8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6}{3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1} = \frac{336}{6} = \textbf{56}



Fifty-six teams. The bottom of the fraction, 3!, removes the orderings that do not count.
